short: Diocletian's edicts began the empire's longest and most severe campaign against Christianity.
full:
On 23 February 303, Diocletian issued the first of four edicts ordering the destruction of churches, the burning of scriptures, the dismissal of Christians from office and, eventually, that all citizens sacrifice to the gods on pain of death. The persecution was enforced with particular severity in the eastern provinces under Galerius and Maximinus Daza, while Constantius in the West applied it lightly, and it produced a wave of martyrdoms and a lasting schism between Christians who had complied and those who had not.

Enforcement varied by region and weakened after Diocletian's abdication in 305, but the campaign continued unevenly for years. It ended when the dying Galerius issued an edict of toleration on 30 April 311, admitting the policy had failed to eradicate the faith. Constantine and Licinius's settlement at Milan in 313 completed the reversal, but it was Galerius's edict that first restored Christians' legal standing after a persecution that had lasted the better part of a decade.
